title: Resistant before the drug arrives?
hook: A dish of bacteria has never met a drug. Could any of them already resist it?

knows: natural selection: variants that survive better leave more offspring
doesNotKnow: that resistant mutants can exist before any drug is used
that a drug selects resistance that was already there rather than creating it

misconception: The drug causes the resistance in the bacteria it meets.
objective: The learner can explain that 10 billion cells at 1 resistant in 100 million already hold about 100 resistant cells; the drug kills the rest, and the survivors regrow, so the drug selects resistance rather than causing it.

claims.text: 10 billion cells x 1 in 100 million = 100 resistant cells expected; 1 billion gives 10, 100 million gives 1, 10 million gives 0.1.
claims.source: 10^10 x 10^-8 = 100 (arithmetic, artifacts/scratch/w2life/check.mjs). The stage shows these expected counts, rounded, not a random draw.

claims.text: Resistance mutations in bacteria arise at random before exposure to a selective agent; the agent selects the mutants that already exist.
claims.source: Luria S.E. & Delbruck M. (1943) Genetics 28:491-511; Lederberg J. & Lederberg E.M. (1952) J. Bacteriol. 63:399-406 (replica plating).

claims.text: 1 in 100 million is an illustrative figure; real mutation frequencies vary widely between genes, drugs and species.
claims.source: Figure chosen in the brief (company/domains/briefs/life.md #17) as a convention. Per-drug frequencies in wild-type E. coli run from about 1e-9 (nalidixic acid) to 1e-7 (rifampicin) depending on assay and strain; a per-drug table should replace the earlier Drake (1991) PNAS 88:7160 citation, which is about per-genome rates.

claims.text: With 0.1 resistant cells expected (10 million cells), a dish usually has none: if resistant cells occur independently, the chance of none is e^-0.1, about 90%.
claims.source: Poisson approximation, P(0) = e^-0.1 = 0.905 (artifacts/scratch/w2life/check.mjs). Real counts fluctuate more (Luria-Delbruck jackpots), which this toy ignores.

claims.text: The dish is a toy: the drug kills every non-resistant cell, the lawn is a texture rather than one dot per cell, and resistant cells sit at positions from an untuned seed (mulberry32(3)).
After the drug, every cell in the regrown dish descends from a survivor, so every cell in it is resistant.
claims.source: Toy-model consequence: the drug kills all non-resistant cells (c5); offspring of resistant cells inherit the mutation.

claims.text: A resistance mutation is a random change in a cell that lets it survive a drug.
claims.source: Standard microbiology definition; Luria & Delbruck (1943) Genetics 28:491-511 (as c2).

recall.question: A drug is added to a huge bacterial culture and a few cells survive and regrow, all resistant. Where did the resistance most likely come from?
options: Rare resistant mutants were already in the culture
Resistance spread from the drug itself
recall.why: In billions of cells, a few already carry a resistance mutation. The drug kills the rest, so the survivors are the mutants that were there before.
